propositions.text: I allow the appeals.
propositions.quote: I allow the appeals.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeals.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant (PA) and Minor Appellant (MA) are Colombian citizens, with PA as MA's mother.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Principal Appellant or PA) and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Minor Appellant or MA) are citizens of Colombia. The PA is the mother of the MA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the PA and MA are Colombian citizens and mother and child.

propositions.text: The Appellants fear their cousin, an influential member in Colombia, due to family conflict involving PA's brother's wrongful conviction.
propositions.quote: The Appellants fear their cousin, Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, an influential member XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) in Colombia. In 2000, the PA's brotherXXXX XXXX XXXX, allowed a friend of XXXXs to live with him. Shortly thereafter, XXXX XXXX, then XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was arrested and detained on charges of kidnapping and extortion. Family conflict ensued, as the PA was the only person to maintain her brother's innocence; she believed that XXXX XXXX was set up by XXXX XXXX In contrast, XXXX openly conveyed to family members that XXXX XXXX was guilty. The PA took active steps to assist in her brother's defence, but in XXXX 2001, XXXX XXXX directed the PA to stop. He did not give an explanation but was so adamant that the PA complied, all the while suspecting that her brother had been threatened by XXXX. In XXXX 2001, XXXX XXXX was convicted and sentenced to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the family conflict and fear of the cousin due to PA's brother's conviction.

propositions.text: In 2008, XXXX was arrested and later released; in 2017, a corruption investigation led to XXXX absconding and threats to PA, prompting the Appellants to flee Colombia in 2018.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2008, XXXX was arrested, due to information received from another relative, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The PA visited XXXX in jail to express satisfaction that he would pay for his nefarious activities. XXXX intimated that he would not be incarcerated for long. Indeed, he was released only four years later, in XXXX 2012. XXXX XXXX was released in XXXX 2012 on good behaviour. In XXXX 2017, a widespread corruption investigation led to the re-opening of XXXXs case and the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX absconded before he could be arrested. In XXXX 2017, XXXX XXXX received phone calls from an angry XXXX XXXX Believing that the PA had provided incriminating information to the authorities through her XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX threatened the PA. When XXXX XXXX relayed these threats to the PA, she decided to flee Colombia. Having already planned to visit relatives in Canada, the Appellants left the country on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 using their visitor's visas.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts arrests, threats, and the Appellants' flight to Canada in 2018.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the Appellants' claims due to PA's lack of credibility and no evidence of XXXX's interest in finding them.
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected the Appellants' claims due to the PA's overall lack of credibility and the lack of any evidence of XXXX's interest in finding them.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claims due to PA's lack of credibility and no evidence of threat interest.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue the RPD erred by focusing on minor discrepancies, speculating XXXX could be dead, and ignoring police report on threats to MA.
propositions.quote: The Appellants contend that the RPD erred by basing its credibility findings on microscopic discrepancies, by unduly speculating that XXXX could be dead, and by assigning no weight to the police report relating to threatening texts sent to the MA.

propositions.text: The Appellants allege the Panel Member showed reasonable apprehension of bias.
propositions.quote: The Appellants further allege that the Panel Member demonstrated a reasonable apprehension of bias.

propositions.text: The Appellants submitted new evidence and request an oral hearing.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have submitted new evidence in this appeal and are requesting an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue RPD erred on credibility, allege bias, submit new evidence, and request oral hearing.

propositions.text: The determinative issue is the Appellants' credibility.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue is the Appellants' credibility.

propositions.text: New evidence is inadmissible and oral hearing is not permitted.
propositions.quote: I have determined that the new evidence is inadmissible, and an oral hearing is not permitted.

propositions.text: After full assessment, Appellants likely face risk to life or cruel treatment and are persons in need of protection under section 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, after a fulsome assessment of the record, I find that the Appellants likely face a risk to their lives, or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and are thus persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds credibility is key, new evidence inadmissible, no oral hearing, but Appellants likely face risk and need protection.

propositions.text: The appeals are allowed and the court substitutes its own decision that Appellants are persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The appeals are allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: The evidence presented by the Appellants is rejected.
propositions.quote: NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellants is rejected

paragraphs.summary: The court allows appeals, substitutes decision finding protection needed, and rejects Appellants' evidence.

propositions.text: Evidence is accepted only if it arose after RPD decision, was not reasonably available then, or could not reasonably be expected to be brought before RPD.
propositions.quote: According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that: (a) arose after the RPD decision; or (b) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (c) that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal criteria for accepting new evidence on appeal.

propositions.text: If evidence meets criteria, court must decide if it is credible, relevant, and new before acceptance; newness is somewhat redundant.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must then decide if the evidence is credible, relevant, and new before I can accept it.2 The newness criterion is somewhat redundant, as it does not add to the explicit requirements of subsection 110(4).3

paragraphs.summary: The court explains further criteria for accepting new evidence: credibility, relevance, and newness.

propositions.text: Appellants submitted PA's affidavit, brother's statement, neighbour's statement, and news articles as new evidence.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Appellants describe the new evidence merely as the "Affidavit of [the PA]".4 In fact, the Appellants have submitted much more. In addition to the PA's affidavit, the Appellants' Record includes: a second sworn statement from the PA's brother (XXXX XXXX), a sworn statement from the PA's neighbour in Colombia, and news articles that explain XXXXs 2008 arrest and XXXX XXXX and that address the problem of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX armed groups.5 For the following reasons, I find that none of this evidence is admissible.

paragraphs.summary: The court lists the new evidence submitted but finds none admissible.

propositions.text: PA's affidavit repeats prior narrative and testimony and contests RPD findings; mostly argument, not new evidence.
propositions.quote: The PA's affidavit of October 12, 2019 repeats her Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, summarizes her oral testimony, and contests the RPD's findings. Rather than new evidence, it consists mostly of arguments that ought to have been raised either at the RPD hearing or in the Appellants' memorandum.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PA's affidavit is mostly argument repeating prior claims, not new evidence.

propositions.text: PA's employment status after claim rejection is new but irrelevant and inadmissible; rest of affidavit not new evidence.
propositions.quote: The one exception is a reference to the fact that the PA works at XXXX and does not rely on social assistance.6 This information did arise after August 16, 2019, the date the asylum claim was rejected; it provides the PA's employment status as of the date the document was sworn. Her employment history in Canada, however, was not an issue at the RPD hearing and is not capable of proving or disproving a fact that is relevant to the Appellants' claims for protection. Given this lack of relevance, the employment update is inadmissible. As stated above, the rest of the affidavit is not new evidence. I will nevertheless consider it as an addendum to the Appellants' Memorandum.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PA's employment update is new but irrelevant and inadmissible; rest of affidavit not new evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellants say brother's new statement is more in-depth and confirms threats against PA.
propositions.quote: The Appellants contend that the October 11, 2019 statement of the PA's brother, XXXX XXXX, is "more in-depth" and "confirm[s] XXXX's threats against the claimant".

propositions.text: The new statement clarifies omissions from previous statement.
propositions.quote: It also serves to clarify omissions from the previous statement.

propositions.text: Claimants must present all relevant evidence to RPD; RAD appeal is not to correct deficient record.
propositions.quote: In advancing claims for refugee protection, the Appellants are responsible for adducing all relevant and available evidence. Claimants must put forward their entire case to the RPD, since an appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is not an opportunity to correct a deficient record.

propositions.text: Brother's original affidavit was included in RPD Record; new statement links threats to PA causing confiscation of assets.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX's original affidavit is included in the RPD Record.10 The one provided in this appeal explicitly links XXXX threats towards the PA to XXXX's belief that the PA caused the confiscation of his assets.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue brother's new statement confirms threats and clarifies omissions; court says all evidence must be presented to RPD, original affidavit was included.

propositions.text: Evidence must postdate claim rejection date; statement dated 2019 refers only to events before rejection and was reasonably available before.
propositions.quote: Though the statement is dated October 11, 2019, it is the facts or circumstances established by the documentary evidence which must postdate the date of the rejection of the claim.11 The date of the statement is not determinative. XXXX XXXX's new statement refers only to events occurring up to XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, while the Appellants still lived in Colombia.

propositions.text: Brother's new statement arose before rejection, was reasonably available, and could have been presented before RPD decision; thus inadmissible.
propositions.quote: Therefore, this evidence arose well before the date of rejection (August 16, 2019). Moreover, it was reasonably available before then, given that XXXX XXXX was able to compose his first statement almost two years earlier, on XXXX XXXX, 2017.12 Lastly, the new evidence contained in the most recent statement could be reasonably expected to have been presented prior to the date of the RPD's decision; it relates to the allegations of harmful threats, which lie at the core of the Appellants' claims. I also note the 18 days between the date of the hearing and the date of the decision; the Appellants have not shown that they even attempted to make an application to submit post-hearing documents, pursuant to Rule 43 of the RPD Rules. Thus, XXXX XXXX's new statement is inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds brother's new statement relates to pre-rejection events, was available before, and is inadmissible.

propositions.text: Neighbour's statement dated 2019 recounts events before rejection, was reasonably available, and is inadmissible.
propositions.quote: Almost identical reasons apply to the sworn statement of the PA's neighbour, also dated October 11, 2019. The document recounts interactions with the PA between 2015 and XXXX 2017, all occurring well before the Appellants' claims were rejected.

propositions.text: Appellants did not explain why neighbour's statement was not reasonably available or could not be expected before rejection; thus inadmissible.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not explained why this statement was not reasonably available before the date of rejection or could not be expected to have been presented before that date. Accordingly, this sworn statement is inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds neighbour's statement recounts pre-rejection events, was available before, and is inadmissible.

propositions.text: News articles dated 2008 and 2018 address central claim questions but arose before rejection, were available, and are inadmissible.
propositions.quote: The news articles are dated XXXX XXXX, 2008 and XXXX XXXX, 2018, and they were both retrieved from the internet.14 They give additional information about XXXXs involvement in XXXX and attest to the potential risk faced by the MA if she returned to Colombia. These documents both address central questions in the Appellants' claims, namely, the identity of the agent of harm and the nature of the risk faced by the Appellants. However, the articles arose well before the date that the Appellants' claims were rejected, were reasonably available before that date, and could be expected to have been presented before that date. Accordingly, they are inadmissible in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds news articles address key issues but are pre-rejection, available, and inadmissible.

propositions.text: The Appellants request an oral hearing and explain why it is needed.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have requested an oral hearing and provided submissions to explain why one is needed.

propositions.text: Under IRPA s.110(6), oral hearing requires admissible new evidence; none exists here, so hearing denied.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, a prerequisite for an oral hearing is admissible new evidence. As there is no such evidence in this appeal, an oral hearing cannot be held. The Appellants' request is therefore denied.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants request oral hearing; court denies it due to lack of admissible new evidence.

propositions.text: RAD reviews RPD decisions independently and may substitute its own decision if assessment differs.
propositions.quote: The RAD reviews RPD decisions by conducting an independent assessment of the refugee claim. If the RAD's assessment differs from that of the RPD, the RAD may substitute its own decision.

propositions.text: If RPD has meaningful advantage in credibility assessment, deference is given; otherwise, correctness standard applies.
propositions.quote: If the RPD has a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral testimony, then the RPD's finding may be accorded deference. Otherwise, the standard of correctness applies.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD's independent review and when deference to RPD applies.

propositions.text: RPD did not have meaningful advantage; court applies correctness standard in independent assessment.
propositions.quote: In this case, the RPD did not have a meaningful advantage. Accordingly, I have conducted an independent assessment of the oral and documentary evidence using the correctness standard.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD had no meaningful advantage and applies correctness standard in assessment.

propositions.text: The RPD's credibility findings were made with a clear apprehension of bias against the claimant.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the RPD's credibility findings were made with a "clear apprehension of bias against the claimant."19

propositions.text: Claimants have the right to be heard and to an impartial decision-maker, critical components of natural justice rules the IRB must follow.
propositions.quote: Claimants have the right to be heard and the right to an impartial decision-maker, rights which are critical components of the rules of natural justice that the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) is bound to follow.20

propositions.text: A reasonable apprehension of bias breaches natural justice by fostering an appearance of unfair proceedings.
propositions.quote: When displaying a reasonable apprehension of bias, a panel member fosters an appearance that the proceedings are unfair, thereby breaching the rules of natural justice.

propositions.text: After reviewing the record, the Appellants' argument of bias is without merit.
propositions.quote: After reviewing the record, I find that the Appellants' argument is without merit.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants allege bias in RPD's credibility findings; the court explains natural justice requires impartiality and finds the allegation without merit.

propositions.text: Counsel did not explain how bias appeared; alleged bias seems tied to aggressive questioning and microscopic credibility findings.
propositions.quote: Counsel did not specifically explain how an appearance of bias was manifested in this case. I gather from the appeal record that the alleged bias is tied to the Panel's aggressive questioning and microscopic credibility findings related to particular omissions in XXXX XXXX's original sworn statement of 2017.

propositions.text: The Appellants rely on Cipak to argue aggressive credibility questioning can create perception of bias when excessive.
propositions.quote: To support their position, the Appellants include the 2014 Federal Court's decision of Cipak in their appeal record.

propositions.text: Justice Roy held that aggressive pursuit of credibility issues beyond their worth can create perception of bias.
propositions.quote: In that decision, Justice Roy held that aggressively pursuing an issue that is purportedly related to credibility can create a perception of bias when the pursuit goes beyond the issue's worth.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes counsel did not specify bias manifestation; Appellants cite Cipak where excessive aggressive questioning caused bias perception.

propositions.text: Cipak facts differ: claimants blamed counsel's translation errors; panel investigated for months and pressed waiver of solicitor-client privilege.
propositions.quote: In Cipak, the claimants explained that the omissions and inconsistencies in their narrative were a result of errors made by their former counsel who translated the document from Slovak to English. The Panel decided to investigate the issue for several months and pressed the claimant to waive solicitor-client privilege.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Cipak facts differ significantly from this case, involving translation errors and prolonged investigation.

propositions.text: This case differs: omission central to claim's risk; panel gave multiple chances to explain omission, which is appropriate.
propositions.quote: This is altogether different than seizing an omission that drives to the heart of the refugee claim (e.g. the nature of the risk of danger) and giving the claimant multiple opportunities to account for the omission, which is precisely what the Panel Member did in this case.

propositions.text: XXXX XXXX's statement omitted alleged threat to PA; ten minutes of hearing questioned PA on this discrepancy.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX's statement did not mention XXXX alleged threat to the PA, and so ten minutes of the hearing was spent on questioning the PA about the discrepancy.

propositions.text: PA required interpreter, making clear and accurate questioning important.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the PA required an interpreter at the hearing, making it especially important for the Panel to take the time to ensure that the questions and responses were clear and accurate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case differs from Cipak; the omission was central, panel gave multiple chances, and interpreter use justified careful questioning.

propositions.text: After full hearing review, no overly aggressive or harsh tone found in panel's questioning.
propositions.quote: After listening to the hearing recording in its entirety, I did not notice any issues with the Panel's questioning, such as an overly aggressive or harsh tone.

propositions.text: Panel member's conduct was appropriate and did not lead to appearance of bias on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: I therefore find that the Panel Member's conduct was entirely appropriate and did not, on a balance of probabilities, lead to an appearance of bias.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no aggressive tone in panel questioning and concludes conduct was appropriate without bias appearance.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellants lacked credibility because PA could not explain omissions in brother's 2017 statement.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellants lacked credibility because the PA could not explain omissions in her brother's statement of XXXX XXXX, 2017.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD's position was unduly microscopic.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' position is that the RPD's position was unduly microscopic.

propositions.text: I agree with Appellants that the RPD erred in this respect.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found lack of credibility due to unexplained omissions; Appellants argue this was microscopic; court agrees RPD erred.

propositions.text: Claimants must explain discrepancies but RPD held PA to unreasonable standard since PA did not write or dictate statement.
propositions.quote: While claimants are expected to explain discrepancies in their evidence, the RPD erred by holding the PA to an unreasonable standard.

propositions.text: PA did not write or dictate statement; brother did not testify and lives in Colombia.
propositions.quote: The PA neither wrote the statement nor claimed to have dictated it to her brother. XXXX XXXX did not testify at the RPD hearing and resides in Colombia.

propositions.text: PA's response that she does not know why brother omitted blaming PA was reasonable under circumstances.
propositions.quote: Under these circumstances, the PA's response was eminently reasonable: she does not know why XXXX XXXX failed to mention the fact that XXXX blames the PA for the confiscation of XXXX's properties.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD held PA to unreasonable standard; PA reasonably could not explain brother's omission as she did not write statement.

propositions.text: Omission does not undermine claimant's overall credibility nor justify assigning statement no weight; RPD erred.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the omission does not undermine the claimant's overall credibility, and it also does not justify assigning the statement no weight. The RPD erred in assessing the Appellants' relocations

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the omission does not undermine credibility or justify no weight; RPD erred.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative inference on PA's credibility due to relocations in BOC not in Schedule A form.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a negative inference as to the credibility of the PA because her BOC asserts that she moved twice before leaving Colombia, while these relocations are not referenced in her Schedule A form.

propositions.text: Appellants contest this finding without providing reasons.
propositions.quote: The Appellants contest this finding, without providing reasons for their position.

propositions.text: After review, I find the RPD erred on this point.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, after reviewing the record, I find that the RPD erred.

paragraphs.summary: RPD negatively inferred PA's credibility from relocation discrepancies; Appellants contest; court finds RPD erred.

propositions.text: PA explained two-week stay with friend in same building not permanent move, so omitted from Schedule A form.
propositions.quote: She testified that for two weeks in XXXX 2017, she spent the nights with her friend, who lived in the same apartment building. Because this was not a permanent move, she did not believe that it was necessary to mention it in the Schedule A form.

propositions.text: BOC wording 'changed houses on two occasions' does not necessarily imply permanent relocation.
propositions.quote: I further note that the precise wording in the BOC indicates that the Appellants "changed houses on two occasions", which does not necessarily imply a permanent relocation.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes PA's reasonable explanation for omission and that BOC wording does not imply permanent moves.

propositions.text: PA omitted second place to avoid detection by agent of harm.
propositions.quote: The PA failed to mention the second place where she stayed in order to avoid detection from the agent of harm.

propositions.text: Discrepancy is not material; negative credibility finding is unwarranted; RPD erred.
propositions.quote: Even so, I still conclude that a negative credibility finding is unwarranted, as the discrepancy does not involve a material portion of the Appellants' claims or their narrative. Therefore, I find that the RPD erred.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PA omitted second place to avoid harm; discrepancy is immaterial; negative credibility finding unwarranted; RPD erred.

propositions.text: Panel placed no weight on police report because PA said it might not relate to claim and could not recall incident dates.
propositions.quote: The Panel placed no weight on the police report because the PA testified that it might not be related to the claim, and the PA could not remember when the incidents alleged in the report occurred.

propositions.text: Appellants claim RPD disregarded police report without valid reason; PA never ruled out XXXX as sender of text messages.
propositions.quote: The Appellants claim that the RPD disregarded this evidence without a valid reason and that the PA never ruled out the possibility that the text messages were sent by XXXX.

propositions.text: I find RPD did not err in weight placed on police report, for different reasons.
propositions.quote: I find, for different reasons, that the RPD did not err in the weight placed on the police report.

paragraphs.summary: Panel gave no weight to police report; Appellants allege error; court finds no error for different reasons.

propositions.text: In 2017, PA reported threatening WhatsApp messages to police but did not suspect sender's identity.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2017, the PA reported to the police that the MA received threatening text messages via WhatsApp. The PA has consistently maintained that she does not know who sent the messages and that she simply submitted the police report as additional evidence of a potential risk faced by the MA if returned to Colombia. When she reported the text messages to the police, the PA was asked whether she had any suspicions regarding the sender's identity. She responded in the negative.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes PA reported threatening messages to police but did not suspect sender's identity.

propositions.text: Text messages do not threaten harm but imply monitoring and outing as XXXX; MA blocked sender; no similar messages after 2017.
propositions.quote: The text messages do not threaten harm to the MA, though they do imply that she is being monitored and that she will be outed as a XXXX. The MA blocked the sender's phone number, and the Appellants have not alleged that they received similar messages between XXXX 2017 and their departure in XXXX 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Text messages imply monitoring and outing but no direct threat; MA blocked sender; no further messages alleged.

propositions.text: RPD's concise reasons were correct: isolated unknown-origin messages insufficient to establish risk or corroborate threats.
propositions.quote: The RPD's reasons were concise, but nevertheless correct: such isolated correspondence of unknown origin is insufficient to establish a risk of harm and, more specifically, fails to corroborate the alleged threats from XXXX.

propositions.text: Police report is credible as contemporaneous account but content is irrelevant to refugee claim issues and has no probative value.
propositions.quote: The police report itself is credible. It offers a contemporaneous account of the Appellants' concerns while they lived in Colombia. However, on a balance of probabilities, the content of the messages is not relevant to any of the issues raised in the Appellants' refugee claims, and thus it carries no probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds police report credible but irrelevant and insufficient to establish risk or corroborate threats.

propositions.text: RPD was correct to assign police report no weight; this does not detract from Appellants' overall credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD was thus correct in assigning the police report no weight, a finding which, to be clear, does not detract from the Appellants' overall credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes RPD correctly assigned no weight to police report without affecting overall credibility.

propositions.text: At RPD hearing, Counsel submitted Appellants met refugee definition under section 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: At the RPD hearing, Counsel submitted that the Appellants exclusively met the refugee definition set out at section 97 of the IRPA.

propositions.text: An independent assessment is required to determine if Appellants are persons in need of protection under section 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: An independent assessment is nevertheless required. After reviewing the entirety of the record, I agree with the Appellants: they are persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel submitted Appellants met refugee definition; court independently assesses and agrees they are persons in need of protection under section 97 IRPA.

propositions.text: Subjective fear not required to qualify as person in need of protection; objective risk to life or cruel treatment must be assessed.
propositions.quote: To qualify as a person in need of protection, subjective fear is not required. Instead, I must objectively assess the risk to life and the risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

propositions.text: Evidence does not show danger of torture; analysis focuses on paragraph 97(1)(b) IRPA risk of cruel and unusual treatment.
propositions.quote: As the evidence does not reveal a danger of torture (i.e. a substantial risk of intentionally severe physical or mental pain or suffering), my analysis will focus on paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states subjective fear is not required; no torture risk found; analysis focuses on risk of cruel and unusual treatment under IRPA.

propositions.text: Central issue is nature of risk faced by Appellants.
propositions.quote: At the heart of this appeal is determining the nature of the risk faced by the Appellants.

propositions.text: PA believes XXXX threatened her because he suspects she caused confiscation of his assets.
propositions.quote: The PA believes that XXXX threatened her because he suspects that she caused his assets to be confiscated.

propositions.text: RPD gave insufficient reasons to rebut presumption of truth; momentary memory lapses do not diminish credibility or show intent to mislead.
propositions.quote: On the facts of this case, the RPD provided insufficient reasons to rebut the presumption of truth. Contrary to the RPD's findings, momentary lapses in remembering the marital status of one's siblings neither diminish overall credibility nor demonstrate an intent to mislead the tribunal.

propositions.text: Relying on PA's credible testimony, Appellants likely face personalized risk to life if returned to Colombia.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I rely on the PA's credible oral testimony to conclude that the Appellants likely face a personalized risk to their lives if returned to Colombia.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the risk nature issue; PA believes XXXX threatened her; court finds RPD insufficiently rebutted truth presumption and concludes risk likely exists.

propositions.text: XXXX XXXX's detailed sworn statement notarized with biometric identity verification enhances credibility.
propositions.quote: I also rely on XXXX XXXX's detailed sworn statement. The credibility of this document is enhanced by the fact that, when it was notarized on January 16, 2018, XXXX XXXX's identity was verified through biometrics.

propositions.text: XXXX XXXX was arrested in 2000, tried to prove innocence, discovered cousin with aliases linked to criminal group.
propositions.quote: According to XXXX XXXX, after being arrested in XXXX 2000, he tried to prove his innocence. The PA initially assisted him in that endeavour. During their investigation, they discovered that their cousin, XXXX XXXX had different aliases and that he was in fact an important member of a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: XXXX XXXX learned arrest was smokescreen to hide XXXX's criminal activities.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX learned that his arrest was a "smokescreen" meant to hide the true nature of XXXX's criminal activities.

propositions.text: XXXX XXXX is only relative who could testify against XXXX if captured; received calls warning to keep quiet and threatening PA and daughters.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX further contends that he is the only relative in Colombia who could potentially testify against XXXX, should XXXX ever be captured. XXXX XXXX indicates that he has received calls telling him to "remember to keep quiet because they know perfectly well where to find [the PA] and her daughters".

paragraphs.summary: The court relies on XXXX XXXX's notarized statement detailing arrest, criminal group links, and threats to him and PA's family.

propositions.text: XXXX XXXX's statement provides important context and an additional dimension to the harm the Appellants face.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX's statement thus provides important context and offers an additional dimension to the harm that the Appellants face;

propositions.text: Paragraph 97(1)(b) of IRPA is engaged if harm depends on a criminal fugitive's subjective loyalty assessment and the agent has means and motivation to carry out the threat.
propositions.quote: paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA is still engaged, provided that the agent of harm has the means and motivation to carry through with the threat.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds XXXX XXXX's statement adds context to the harm faced and that paragraph 97(1)(b) IRPA applies if harm depends on a fugitive's loyalty and threat capability.

propositions.text: The MA is 15, lives with the PA, and the PA's risk extends to the MA.
propositions.quote: The MA is 15 years old and resides exclusively with the PA; the MA's father is not an active part of her life.

propositions.text: Child Guideline requires reliance on objective evidence for children's claims due to their limited appreciation of harm gravity.
propositions.quote: I have considered the Child Guideline, and recognize that the objective evidence must be relied upon when deciding a child's claim because children often do not appreciate the gravity of the harm that they face.

propositions.text: Given XXXX's influence, cohabitation, and threats referencing PA's daughters, harm to PA likely includes harm to MA.
propositions.quote: Given XXXX's ongoing influence in XXXX XXXX, the fact that the Appellants' live together, and XXXX's express reference to the PA's daughters in his veiled threats, any harm aimed at the PA would likely be inflicted on the MA as well.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the MA is 15, lives with the PA, and likely shares the PA's risk due to XXXX's influence and threats.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, the Appellants' lives would be in danger if returned to Colombia; XXXX and associates are agents of harm.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants' lives would be in danger if they returned to Colombia. The agent of harm is XXXX, along with his former associates in the XXXX.

propositions.text: A 2008 judgment identified XXXX as a criminal figure; PA's cousin's husband testified against XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds on balance of probabilities that XXXX and associates threaten the Appellants' lives, supported by evidence of criminal activity, family ties, and threats.

propositions.text: XXXX continues to have means and motivation to harm Appellants if returned; familial connection aids locating them.
propositions.quote: I have reached the conclusion that XXXX continues to have the means and motivation to harm the Appellants if they returned. Though XXXX remains at large and the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the metastasizing nature of Colombian XXXX XXXX gives him the ability to easily pursue the Appellants. Their familial connection provides an additional route for XXXX to locate the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes XXXX still has means and motivation to harm the Appellants, with family ties facilitating locating them.

propositions.text: PA's brother and XXXX are XXXX XXXX XXXX; XXXX has connections in Colombian government and drug trafficking.
propositions.quote: The PA's brother and XXXX are both XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX continues to have connections within the Colombian government and drug trafficking organizations.

propositions.text: Witness protection programs in Colombia are limited, subject to annual review, subcontracted, and restrict liberties, causing some to avoid participation.
propositions.quote: Witness protection programs are limited in the country, as protection measures are subject to annual re-evaluation and can be subcontracted to private companies. Participating in these programs also significantly restricts one's liberties; conduct such as tending to an ill relative can lead to expulsion.

propositions.text: PA's cousin refrained from joining witness protection due to restrictions; other cousins sought asylum in Canada after program ended.
propositions.quote: These types of restrictions caused the PA's cousin, XXXX XXXX, to refrain from joining the program. Even though the PA's other cousins did participate in it, they successfully sought asylum in Canada as soon as the program ended.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Colombian witness protection is limited and restrictive, with some family members avoiding it and others seeking asylum in Canada.

propositions.text: Evidentiary record shows no adequate state protection and no safe alternative location in Colombia for Appellants.
propositions.quote: Under these circumstances, I find that the evidentiary record demonstrates that adequate state protection would not be forthcoming and that the Appellants would not be safe in any other location in Colombia.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no adequate state protection or safe alternative location in Colombia for the Appellants.

propositions.text: The RPD's finding that the Appellants' Colombian nationality is established is agreed with.
propositions.quote: I agree with the RPD's finding that the Appellants' identities as nationals of Colombia are established.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the RPD that the Appellants' Colombian nationality is established.

propositions.text: The Appellants are persons in need of protection under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellants are persons in need of protection under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellants are persons in need of protection under paragraph 97(1)(b) IRPA.

propositions.text: The appeals are allowed; the RPD determination is set aside and replaced with a finding that the Appellants need protection under paragraph 97(1)(b) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The appeals are allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, I set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute my own determination that the Appellants are persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeals, sets aside the RPD decision, and finds the Appellants need protection under paragraph 97(1)(b) IRPA.
